analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 30% minimum federal tax on households earning over $1 million a year.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 15 Democratic and Independent cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has received no vote or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a new minimum tax: anyone with yearly income over $1 million would owe at least 30% of their income in federal taxes, after allowing charitable deductions and counting payroll taxes they already paid. The tax phases in just above the $1 million mark and the threshold rises with inflation. The bill's stated purpose is to make sure the highest earners cannot pay lower tax rates than middle-income families, and to cut the deficit by billions of dollars a year.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the federal Treasury would collect billions more a year from roughly the top fraction of one percent of earners, reducing deficits that otherwise burden everyone. Households earning under $1 million would owe nothing new. The bill also states a goal of spurring broader tax reform that closes loopholes used by the wealthiest taxpayers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a tax equal to 30% of a high earner's adjusted gross income (minus a modified charitable contribution deduction) whenever that exceeds the amount they owe under the regular income tax, the alternative minimum tax, and payroll taxes combined.

The tax only applies to taxpayers with adjusted gross income over $1,000,000 ($500,000 for married people filing separately), with the threshold adjusted for inflation after 2025, and it phases in gradually just above that threshold so incomes near $1 million are not hit with a sudden cliff.

The bill's own 'sense of the Senate' section describes it as an interim step that would set a floor on taxes for the highest earners and cut the deficit by billions of dollars a year while broader tax reform is considered.

analysis.who_pays: Households with adjusted gross income above $1 million a year — about the top 0.5% of filers — would pay more, most sharply those whose income comes from capital gains, carried interest, and other forms now taxed at lower rates than wages. The tax counts what they already pay in payroll taxes, so it targets people whose total tax rate currently falls below 30%.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds a third parallel tax computation alongside the regular income tax and the existing alternative minimum tax, adding complexity to an already complicated code and creating extra compliance work for high-income filers and their accountants.

The bill only partially preserves the charitable contribution deduction against the new minimum tax (the deduction is prorated and zero for non-itemizers), so a good-faith objection is that it could reduce large charitable gifts from the very donors who make most big ones.

Supporters of lower rates on investment income argue a minimum tax that effectively reaches capital gains and carried interest could discourage investment, though the bill text does not address this and the provided sources contain no analysis of economic effects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: more revenue from a small, wealthy group versus somewhat higher effective rates on investment income and added tax-complexity. The charitable-deduction treatment is awkwardly designed, but the overall mechanism is simple and targeted. The bigger practical cost is political: with no Republican support, the bill is unlikely to move, so its main real-world effect so far is as a statement of priorities rather than a change in anyone's taxes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill in the Senate on April 1, 2025, joined by 14 Democratic senators and one Independent (Sen. Bernie Sanders).
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action since.
All 15 cosponsors are Democrats or Independents; no Republican has signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one's taxes have changed: the bill has not advanced. Households earning over $1 million are better off in the practical sense that the 30% minimum tax has not moved toward law, and its Senate committee has not taken it up.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, since the bill hasn't advanced

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors are Democrats or Independents and there is no recorded Republican support; no roll-call vote has occurred.

industries.industry: Households earning over $1 million a year
industries.note: These taxpayers would owe a minimum 30% of income in federal taxes, eliminating the advantage of lower rates on capital gains and other investment income. Their interest in the bill's defeat runs against the deficit reduction everyone else would fund through it.

industries.industry: Private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital managers
industries.note: Managers whose income is carried interest taxed at preferential rates would owe the minimum tax on it, erasing much of that advantage. The public pays for the resulting revenue otherwise lost to the Treasury.

The bill allows a charitable deduction against the new minimum tax, but only a prorated one and none for non-itemizers, which could modestly reduce very large charitable gifts while preserving most of the incentive.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Finance Committee with no Republican cosponsors and no scheduled action. Similar minimum-tax-on-millionaires proposals in past Congresses died in committee. Unless it is attached to a larger tax or budget bill, it is likely to remain in committee through the 119th Congress.
